tip: 'Ska' plus an infinitive expresses plans and intentions: 'jag ska åka' = I'm going to go. One of the most common ways to talk about the future.
'Hade' plus the form used after 'har' makes had done: 'hade stått' = had stood, an action before another point in the past.
'Skulle vilja' is a polite way to make a request: 'vi skulle vilja boka' = we would like to book.
'Sjön' and 'solen' show 'the' with just an ending; the extra 'den'/'det' is only needed when an adjective comes before the noun.
For habitual or general statements the '-s' passive is the usual choice: 'maten lagas av kocken' adds '-s' to the verb instead of using 'bli'.
'Har' plus an '-s' form makes has been done: 'boken har översatts' = the book has been translated.
'Dit' means 'to where' and marks motion: 'platsen dit vi reste'. 'Där' means 'where' for a static location.
The '-s' on 'öppnas' makes it passive: the door is opened. Some verbs always end in '-s' without being passive; context tells you which.
'Kvar' means left or remaining. 'Stannar kvar' means stays behind or lingers, adding the sense of not going away.
When 'som' is the object of the clause you can drop it: 'parken vi besöker' means the same as 'parken som vi besöker'.
Swedish uses one word, 'som', for both who and that: 'människor som pratar' = people who talk, and the same 'som' works for things.
The past passive adds '-s' to the past tense: 'bokade' plus '-s' gives 'bokades', meaning was booked, with no helper verb.
'Det som' means what, in the sense of the thing that: 'det som gör' = what makes.
'Som spelas' = that is being played; the '-s' passive is very natural inside a 'som' clause.
'Den som' means whoever or the one who: 'den som frågar' = whoever asks, used for general statements.
'Vars' means whose: 'mannen vars hund' = the man whose dog. It never changes form.
'Blev' plus a form like 'öppnad' builds a passive for one completed event, unlike the '-s' passive for general facts.
'Under' with a time span means over or during: 'under två år' = over a period of two years, not underneath anything.
In a passive, 'av' marks who does the action: 'talas av tio miljoner' = spoken by ten million.
Inside a 'som' clause words like 'aldrig' (never) come before the verb: 'jag aldrig har sett', not 'jag har aldrig sett' as in a main clause.
'Allt som allt' is a set phrase meaning all in all or all things considered. It is not read literally.
'Så vitt jag vet' is a fixed phrase for as far as I know. 'Vitt' here is not the color white.
'Inte förrän' means not until. Starting a sentence with it flips verb and subject, so it is 'fick vi', not 'vi fick'.
'Ha på sig' is the idiom for wearing clothes: 'hon har på sig' = she has on, meaning she is wearing.
'Träffas' ends in '-s' to mean meet each other. The '-s' gives a mutual sense, so 'vi träffas' = we meet up.
Swedish uses 'på' for days and holidays: 'på julafton' = on Christmas Eve, just as 'på söndag' = on Sunday.
'Varannan' means every other: 'varannan dag' = every other day, alternating between on days and off days.
Adding '-tiden' to a clock hour means around that time: 'vid åttatiden' = around eight, not exactly eight.
'Brukade' plus an infinitive means used to: 'brukade besöka' = used to visit, for a past habit that has stopped.
For a place, use 'där' (where) instead of 'som': 'stugan där vi brukade bo' = the cabin where we used to live.
